text: Let's begin our Lesson 5 on building your morning routine.

In this lecture, you'll learn what a morning routine is, the problem with having no morning routine, what makes a successful morning routine, the solution—the Warm Up engine—and talk a little bit about the night and day routine at the end.
First of all, we will talk just a little bit about what a morning routine is.
I guess everybody kind of knows what a morning routine is, but
a morning routine is a series of steps which you do every day, every morning, to kickstart your day.

A morning routine can be something like getting out of bed and making your bed, washing your face and brushing your teeth, drinking a glass of water, doing a quick stretch or short walk, eating a simple breakfast, reviewing your top three priorities for the day, and starting your first important task.
Or they can also just be way much longer,
or way much shorter.
It can be having multiple things; it can even be having journaling, working out, reading—all different types of stuff, all different types of routines which people have.
The problem with no morning routine is that, first of all, you start your day with low energy and no clear direction.
What really happens when you don't have a morning routine, usually, is just that you don't know where to start.
You know, it's like you know what to do,
but sometimes, what I like to call the morning routine is like the engine—the engine which makes you do the work, makes you run for the rest of the day.
And you kind of have to turn on the engine, of course, so that you work.
Just like for a car to work, you have to turn on the car.
And when you don't really have a morning routine, the thing is that, most of the time, you're going to start with low energy, in a direction which is not clear,
no matter what time it is going to happen.

Even though what we did in the previous lecture is going to make that so much rarer if you go and do the steps which we have taught, if you have broken down the big goal all the way to where you have exactly the task you're going to do today.
But the morning routine is that kind of engine.
The second thing is that you waste time deciding what to do instead of starting.
Again, this hopefully will
rely on us knowing exactly what we're going to do today.
But again, there are still going to be days where you're going to waste time deciding what to do.
Instead, with the morning routine, you immediately start.

Because even if you sometimes don't know, or if it's not a strong enough idea of what exactly you are going to do, the morning routine will help you do that—will help you get started because it's something where you know,
your brain knows, because it's something which repeats every single day and you know exactly what you're going to do.
And you don't have to force your mind; you don't have to make your mind remember where to start or something like this, because you know exactly where you're going to start.
The third thing is: you delay important work and feel resistance to starting.
Again, this ties back to the point of having that
engine.
When you don't fire up that engine, trying to stay in your mind—trying to force your mind to immediately go to the deep work session, to immediately do the big tasks—is going to be so much harder.
You know, it's like you have to warm up your engine.
You have to even wake up a little bit, even though, if you can definitely go straight to work, do that.
And we will talk about how one of the reasons why we make a morning routine is to go straight to the
important task or to the work which you have to do.
But mostly, when you don't really have a morning routine, you kind of delay your work because you don't really know what to do.

You know, you wake up, but sometimes you feel lazy, sometimes you don't have motivation, and then you're like, "Let me just stay on my phone, let me just stay on my TV, let me just have a little bit of rest right now," which—there's nothing bad about having rest, but again, you're delaying the work
which you should do in the morning so that you can have a free day onward.
And the other thing is that you react to messages, notifications, and distractions.

Again, this also links with the point above: that when you don't have something embedded in your mind—you can see this as a code that you have in your mind that, whatever happens, I will do the morning routine—and then when you have that code in your mind, you block all of the notifications, as we will talk about how exactly
I do.

unimportant and low-value activities.

The likelihood of you just pushing off the big, important task is going to be so much higher, because, again, for most people, to immediately go to work is going to be a little bit difficult, and to be disciplined with that is going to be so much more difficult to do every single day—to go straight to work.
And then what happens is this one simple thing which pulls you away when you wake up, because when you wake up, we

place.
And again, when you don't have a morning routine, you're most likely to go and do some other stuff which is not really something you should do—you know, there's more important stuff to do that day.
And the other thing is that your focus and discipline are inconsistent day-to-day.

wake up, you'll feel low energy.

And the last thing is that your work feels
scattered and more stressful than it should be.

And so for that, we will need to make a morning routine.
But before we make a morning routine, we have to know some points of what makes a successful morning routine.
A successful morning routine is a routine which wakes up the engine which does the work.
The first point is: the morning routine should be simple and short.
It should be easy to remember and execute.
It should be able to reduce decision fatigue.
The morning routine, the simpler it is, the shorter it is, the better it is going to be.
The second point is: it should be repeatable.
Whatever happens in your life, you know that you can do your morning routine,
whatever happens.
You know that your morning routine is going to be so easy to do.
You know it's going to be something which you can do, even if you feel like not doing anything today; the morning routine is that easy that you can definitely do it.
And it's tied to making it simple and short.
When you make it simple and short, of course, it is going to be easy to do.
The third point is: it should be consistent.
You know, it can be, for example, the same time when you wake up, the same order, and establishing a predictable daily rhythm.
It should be something where it's done consistently.
You know, you know exactly what you're going to do, you know where you're going to do it, you know what you're going to do.
So it should be something where you can do it consistently without a problem, no matter what.
Even if you had a bad day yesterday and today you just feel like not doing it, you didn't sleep well, whatever—it's so simple, it's so short, that it's so easy to do.
The fourth point is that your morning routine should be able to give you
energy.
That's also a big point in making your morning routine: that it should kind of wake you up.

It should give you that big start of an engine, where you go from the point of sleeping, where your mind doesn't really know what is going on, to when you finish the morning routine, you're completely awake, you know exactly what to do, you know exactly what is going on, so you have energy.
So your morning routine should give you energy,
both physically, mentally, and spiritually.
The fifth point is: your morning routine should give you focus.
It is a crucial, crucial part.
Not just to have, let's say, just a morning routine—just something to wake up and keep it simple and short—but it should also be something which leads you to focus for the rest of the day.
It gives you something where you know where you're going to go, you know what you're going to do for the rest of the day—even though you know the tasks you have to do, but
it should leave you with complete focus, knowing what to do.
It should minimize distractions and direct attention to your key priorities.
And the last point, which is so crucial again, is that your morning routine needs to lead you to work, needs to lead you to productivity.
It needs to bring you to the most important tasks which we have to do.
So from the time you wake up, and then using your morning
routine to the time you finish your morning routine, you find yourself at work, you find yourself doing the productive thing which you have to do that day.
So again, a successful morning routine is something which is simple and short—the simpler it is, the better; the shorter it is to do, the better as well.
But it should also be repeatable and consistent.
You should be able to do it every single day, whatever happens.
And again, if it's simple and short, it's going to be so much easier to
do.
Your morning routine should warm up the engine, should give you the energy.
Your morning routine should give you the focus, should lead you straight to work.
